runs.analysis: A has broader coverage (nine omissions), well grounded in plan figures, but several omissions overlap with existing roles, and most of its potential_improvements are generic project-management boilerplate (KPIs, reporting cadence, succession, hiring criteria). It misses maritime traffic and a legal lead. B is more concise and more insightful: it catches maritime traffic safety in the Strait, a legal and contract lead, a Chief Engineer for technical governance, monitoring integration and digital twin, climate adaptation ownership, and consortium-government escalation. These are plan-specific and decision-useful. B misses supply chain, QA and a risk officer, but overall its quality and specificity are higher.

Candidate A is more plan-specific and consistent. Its omissions (energy, cybersecurity, maritime traffic, legal, decommissioning, stakeholder engagement) are tied to the project's own facts, and it acknowledges which responsibilities existing roles already hold. Its improvements are substantive: a Chief Engineer, integrated structural–geotechnical monitoring, climate adaptation ownership, and consortium–government escalation. Minor flaw: it says "eight directors" but lists five. Candidate B has detailed omissions, but it contradicts itself by listing supply chain among the existing roles while claiming a Supply Chain Director is missing. Most of its improvements are generic project-management boilerplate (hiring criteria, KPIs, reporting cadence, succession). The cross-border standards interface item is a good catch. B is also very verbose.

A is broader and more tightly tied to the plan's decisions, gates and assumptions. It catches key gaps that B misses: tenant and revenue gate ownership, sovereign hardware provenance, operations readiness, decision authority and governance, and Phase 1 acceptance criteria. Its weaknesses are over-prescription (many new full-time roles), some overlap between items, and minor inconsistencies such as linking the Phase 0 budget to brownfield remediation. B is concise and proportionate, and its construction management gap is real. But it is thinner and omits the tenant, security-provenance and governance gaps that matter most for this plan.

Candidate A gives 4 omissions and 4 improvements. They are concise and tied to plan specifics (Decision 2, the buffer holding cost, the 75% local-hiring mandate, the €4.32B FX variance). The construction role is a real gap. However, the water-expert omission overlaps with the existing Cooling Engineer, and the QA/QC recommendation is awkward because it assigns QA to the Strategist. A misses the tenant and revenue gating owner, operations handoff, and project controls. Candidate B is more comprehensive, with 5 omissions and 10 improvements. It cites plan content throughout, and it identifies gaps that matter for this plan: tenant and revenue commitment ownership, security hardware provenance for DGSI/ANSSI, operations and commissioning, fiber right-of-way, project controls, risk and gate auditing, and governance and decision authority. It also proposes concrete acceptance criteria such as PUE thresholds that trigger Phase 2. Its weaknesses are team bloat from many added FTEs, some overlap (hedging and sovereignty appear twice), a few possibly invented details, and no construction management role. Overall B is more decision-useful for downstream stages, so it wins narrowly.

I can't see the team file, so I judged how well each candidate fits the plan and the team it describes. Candidate A cites named team members and specific plan decisions and risks, which suggests it read the team document closely. Its omissions are material: no program director or PMO, no independent audit function, no stakeholder communications owner, no owner for the €900M of capacity-building grants, and no post-launch data-quality monitoring. Its improvements find real ownership ambiguities, such as Emergency Float drawdown authority, the standards-to-testing handoff, accessibility split across roles, Public Reference Distributor governance, reduction-card negotiation and enforcement of the "three strikes" policy. Each recommendation names owners, timings and triggers, so downstream stages can use it. Its weaknesses are length and a tendency to add FTEs that may overlap existing roles. Candidate B is shorter and shallower. Some items are low-value, such as a logistics assistant and a standards maintenance engineer. Its fund-manager point reallocates work to the Financial Specialist rather than finding a true gap. Some recommendations are vague, and one refers to another stage. It misses the PMO gap and the float governance ambiguity. It does flag the audit gap and the accessibility coordination gap, but with less depth. A is stronger overall.

Candidate A is concise and tied to plan decisions and risks, but its omissions are mostly minor (a logistics assistant, a vague "undefined relationship" item) and it misses larger structural gaps: no PMO or program director, no communications lead, and no clear owner for the €900M capacity-building programme. Candidate B finds those larger gaps, plus the lack of an independent audit function and of post-launch data-quality monitoring for the T+5 latency target. Its improvements use the named team members and cover concrete ownership ambiguities: Emergency Float authority, the standards-to-testing handoff, accessibility integration, reduction-card negotiation, governance of the Public Reference Distributor, and operational ownership of enforcement. B is verbose, invents some thresholds, and adds headcount without weighing the cost. Even so, it is more insightful, specific and useful for downstream planning.

Candidate A is more thorough and decision-useful. It identifies five concrete gaps: QA/vendor audit, real-time KPI monitoring, municipal departmental liaison, volunteer coordination, and learning/after-action capture. Each gap comes with a cost and FTE estimate and is tied to the M2/M4 gates. Its improvements are specific and actionable. They cover a decision matrix, cross-training for single-person roles, a comms cadence, a budget authority matrix, risk owners, a GDPR paper-to-digital migration protocol, contractor SOWs, and partner SLA monitoring. They are grounded in plan details such as Leipzig-Grünau, the paper logs held until the CRM audit at M2, and the five single-resource roles. Weaknesses: some items are generic management hygiene, and it adds many roles, which risks bloating a staffing-constrained plan. It also uses "ADA-compliant", a US term, in an EU context, and the volunteer role is conditional. Candidate B is concise and has a few sensible points, such as a finance tracker, surge volunteer coverage, sampling QA, and a shift to SLA enforcement after M2. It is thin, though, with only 3 omissions and 3 improvements. It also has a sloppy placeholder reference ("Decision X"), vague references ("Review Issue 3"), and little cost or staffing detail. Overall A is more useful for downstream planning despite some bloat.

The team file isn't shown, so I judged both reviews on internal plausibility and how well they fit the plan. Candidate A is concise (3 omissions, 3 improvements) and ties to the M2/M4 gates, tranche tracking and home-kit QA. But it has visible sloppiness: a "Decision X" placeholder, inconsistent role numbering ("Legal Officer 5" vs "Contractor 5"), and a vague "This usually means…". Its role labels (Contract Manager FTE 3, contractors numbered up to 8) may not match the actual team, since B refers to a "Partnership Manager" and five contractors. Some recommendations are weak: having the Incident Commander personally approve all misinformation statements creates a bottleneck, and a quarterly script review is marginal. It misses singleton-role risk, role boundaries and internal-department friction. Candidate B is much more thorough (5 omissions, 11 improvements) with concrete roles, FTE and cost figures, and owners. It covers real team gaps: QA of installations, real-time KPI monitoring for the gate metrics, a municipal-department liaison, volunteer coordination (conditional), after-action ownership, backups for singleton roles, a decision matrix, a budget authority matrix, risk owners and contractor SOWs. It cites plan-specific details such as the Leipzig-Grünau staging base, Decision 9 and Decision 11, and the risk numbers. Its weaknesses: some generic management boilerplate (training framework, performance metrics), the US term "ADA-compliant", length, and added part-time roles that could strain the budget. Overall B is more specific, more decision-useful and more complete; A is tidier but thinner, with a placeholder and a likely wrong role reference.
